name: Canon — the HN video canon as a personal watch-checklist
one_liner: Canon turns the 6,454 videos Hacker News has recommended over 20 years into a ranked, tickable canon: drop your Google Takeout watch history (or just tick by hand) and get "you've seen 37 of the HN 250", a shareable card, and one new talk waiting for you every Monday.
problem: Engineers and curious technical people have a vague sense that there is a canon of great talks and lectures — Alan Kay, Rich Hickey, Feynman, Bret Victor, SICP — but no way to know what's in it or how much of it they've actually seen. Today they browse an "awesome-talks" GitHub list, open four tabs, watch none, and forget it. Karpathy's HackerTube (1 Nov 2026) finally made the underlying signal public: ~40,000 HN comments filtered to 6,454 videos, shipped with a downloadable data zip and an explicit invitation to build your own version. But HackerTube is a browsing feed — sorted by topic and recency, no ranking by how many distinct humans recommended a video, no notion of what you have already watched, no reason to come back on Tuesday. Canon takes the same data and makes it personal and finite: a ranked top-250 canon, your completion percentage, and a weekly one-video assignment.
target_customer: Hacker News readers, backend/infra/ML engineers and CS students — the crowd that put HackerTube at 1,716 points and 452 comments in a day, and that already spawned HackerBooks and HackerTools clones. They hang out on HN, r/programming, X dev-twitter and Lobsters. Free and open source; no buyer.
why_now: Karpathy published HackerTube on 1 Nov 2026 with the filtered dataset as a downloadable zip at hackertube.org/data plus a DATA.md and an explicit "point your Claude at it and ask for your own version" (https://x.com/karpathy/status/2116957135661945283, https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/hacker-tube/). That dataset did not exist a week ago: filtering 43M HN comments for genuine video recommendations was the expensive part, and it has now been done once, publicly. Two derivative sites (HackerBooks, HackerTools) appeared within 48 hours, which shows the remix window is open right now and also that nobody has yet taken the personal/completion angle. The HN Algolia API (free, 10k req/hr, no key) covers the weekly refresh.
comparables: HackerTube itself (https://hackertube.org/) — browse/topic feed, local-session state, sortable by "recently recommended", but confirmed to have no recommendation-count ranking and no watched checklist or weekly arrivals feed. HackerBooks (by roansh) and HackerTools (by @shouvik12, https://dev.to/shouvik12/first-hackertube-then-hackerbooks-now-hackertools-1c9m) are community-wide ranked catalogs with no personal layer. awesome-talks / programming-talks / awesome-tech-talks on GitHub (https://github.com/vkhorikov/awesome-talks, https://github.com/hellerve/programming-talks) are static hand-maintained lists, never ranked by real signal, never tracked. Tech Talks Weekly (https://www.techtalksweekly.io/about) is a weekly newsletter of NEW talks, not a canon and not a tracker. iCheckMovies and Letterboxd prove the "tick off a canon, post your %" behaviour works, but nothing equivalent exists for talks or for YouTube; I could not find a single free tool producing a "34/100 seen" card for any tech list. Gap: ranked canon + personal completion + weekly return, all client-side.
market_note: Not a market; a free open-source project. Hosting is a static page plus one JSON file; a nightly GitHub Action does the refresh. Estimated running cost under $5/month (domain aside). Value is reputation and reuse.
risks: The derivative wave is already crowded (HackerBooks, HackerTools in 48 hours) — a fourth "Hacker{Noun}" lands as noise unless the personal completion card is the headline, not the catalog. The Takeout path adds friction and could confuse people into thinking it uploads their data. And a canon is finite: once you've ticked your 37, the weekly drop has to be genuinely good or you never return.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) The HackerTube zip actually contains per-video recommendation counts (or at least one row per recommending comment, from which counts can be derived) and usable titles — reported to ship with a DATA.md but I could not inspect the schema; fallback is to rebuild counts from the HN Algolia API by searching comments for youtube.com/youtu.be links, which is free and well documented. 2) Enough people will bother to run a Google Takeout export; mitigated by making manual ticking the default path and Takeout the power-user upgrade. 3) Redistributing HN comment snippets alongside the videos is not clearly licensed — mitigated by quoting one short line and always linking back to the HN thread, same as HackerTube does.
first_customers: The 452 people in the HackerTube HN thread (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50319510) — reply there with the link; Show HN the next morning; post on X as a reply to Karpathy's thread and standalone with a screenshot of a 37/250 card; r/programming and Lobsters; the awesome-talks repo issue trackers.
validation_test: Post one image — a mock Canon card reading "I've seen 37 of the HN 250 — my weakest decade: 2010s systems talks" — as a reply in the HackerTube HN thread and on X, with the link. Pass: 150+ clicks and at least 15 people posting their own number within 48 hours. Fail: under 40 clicks, which means the canon framing doesn't land and the idea should stay a browsing tool.
build_plan: Stack: one static page (TypeScript + vanilla DOM or Vite), hosted on GitHub Pages or Vercel; data as a prebuilt canon.json; one nightly GitHub Action for the refresh. No user accounts, no backend, no model call at runtime. Steps: (1) Pull the HackerTube zip from hackertube.org/data, read DATA.md, and aggregate to distinct-recommender counts per video; if the counts aren't in there, rebuild from the free HN Algolia API (hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search_by_date?tags=comment, filtered for youtube links, 10k req/hr, no key). (2) Cut to a ranked top 250 with 12 decade/topic shelves, each entry carrying title, year, HN recommendation count, one quoted line from a recommending comment and the HN thread link. (3) Build the checklist UI: tick by hand, state in localStorage, a live "37 / 250" dial and per-shelf bars. (4) Add the Takeout drop-zone: user drops watch-history.json, parsed entirely in-browser, matched on YouTube video ID, auto-ticks — with a visible "this file never leaves your laptop" line. (5) Render the share card to canvas and offer Download PNG + Copy post text. (6) Weekly: the nightly Action re-queries Algolia for new YouTube recommendations, and Monday's build surfaces "this week's arrival" plus "your next unwatched one". Cut for v1: search, comments, playback inside the app, accounts, Longs, any LLM call at runtime, any non-YouTube source.
launch_post:
Karpathy dropped the HN video data, so I ranked it.

Canon: the 250 videos Hacker News has recommended most in 20 years, as a checklist.

Tick what you've seen (or drop your YouTube Takeout and it ticks itself, locally). Get your %, your weakest shelf, and one new talk every Monday.

Free, open source.
reasoning:
Canon won because it is the only candidate where a genuinely new public asset — Karpathy's filtered HN video dataset, published 1 Nov 2026 with an explicit invitation to remix — meets a personal, postable output. The derivative wave (HackerBooks, HackerTools within 48 hours) proves the data is spreading but also proves everyone is building the same thing: another ranked community catalog. Canon deliberately goes the other way, from catalog to mirror: the output is your number, not the list. That is what makes it shareable and what gives it a second visit. It does not repeat any library idea — the closest is Hiringscope (paste yourself, get scored against public data), but that serves job seekers with HN "Who is hiring" posts and has no canon, no checklist, no tracking over time; Canon serves curious engineers with a video dataset and is built around returning. It is a weekend for this builder: a static page, one prebuilt JSON, one GitHub Action, no model call at runtime, all within TypeScript and static-site skills. could_grow is false — it is a free artifact, and the obvious monetisation (another "Letterboxd for X") is a worse business than it is a gift. Score held back from 9 by two honest gaps: the zip's schema is unverified (hence buildability 8, not 9) and nobody has demonstrated weekly return for a talks canon (hence usefulness 7).

candidates_considered:
VENTURE
(the venture scout did not finish)

PROJECT
1. Canon — HN's 6,454 recommended videos ranked into a tickable top-250 with Takeout auto-ticking and a weekly arrival. PICK: freshest dataset on the internet this week, personal output, a real return reason.
2. HN Mirror — paste your HN username, get everything you've ever recommended (books, videos, tools) as a personal shelf. Finalist; lost because only HN commenters with history can use it (tiny addressable set) and the Algolia-only build gives a thinner output than Canon; worth keeping as a Canon feature later.
3. Watch Debt — drop your YouTube Takeout and see total hours watched vs. the HN canon you skipped. Finalist; lost because it's a guilt-trip stat with no second visit, and TubeTrace already analyses Takeout history.
4. Fontsmith — DeepSeek V4.1 Flash generating a custom font per prompt (from @nutlope's $0.02 fonts post). Dropped at screen: model outputs text/SVG only, so compiling a real .ttf needs a toolchain, and nutlope is open-sourcing 36 fonts on Monday — building adjacent to that is building into his launch.
5. Spiderpart — exploded procedural-part renderer from one photo, inspired by @elvar_official's Claude skill. Dropped: near-identical to Exploded already in the library.
6. Growth Board — the fastest-growing startups on X by follower growth as a live weekly leaderboard (@benln). Dropped at screen: requires paid X API access at any real scale; the data is the whole product and it's the expensive part.
7. Creator Floor — cheap UGC-creator discovery surfaced as a public "small creators with outsized engagement" board (@shengkunye). Dropped: the source project is itself open source and free, so this is a thin skin on someone's launch.
8. Caro Cuts — turn a long podcast into chaptered, quotable clips using the timestamp structure (@dwarkesh_sp). Dropped at screen: video processing needs a real backend and the space is crowded with paid clip tools.
9. Coldread — paste your site, see which ICP an outreach agent would infer about you (Explee). Dropped: too close to a venture-side sales-tooling idea and the output is not postable.
10. Agent Drift Diary — track how an agent's answers to the same prompt change week to week. Dropped: overlaps Driftwatch and Voiceprint in the library.
research_notes:
Venture: 

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised HackerTube's premise and confirmed the data zip exists and is downloadable; checked DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on Together (real, $0.30/$1.20 per M tokens, released 10 Sep 2026, updated 1017 build 16 Oct — but text-only output, which killed the font candidate); tried to get the zip's schema and learned the post doesn't publish it, which is why buildability caps at 8 and the build plan carries an Algolia fallback.
Screening pot (5/5): checked for an existing personalized HN-recommendation tool (none found); an AI font generator (crowded and not the right output modality); existing HackerTube remixes (found HackerBooks and HackerTools — confirmed both are community catalogs, no personal layer); YouTube-playlist-to-curriculum tools (several paid study tools, none canon-based); and a general "how many have you seen" card tool (iCheckMovies and Letterboxd in film, nothing in tech). This is what pushed the idea from "another catalog" to "your completion of a canon".
Deep research pot (8/8): verified the HackerTube data page and that the site shows recommending comments; confirmed HackerTube has no count-ranking, no watched marker, no weekly feed (only a "recently recommended" sort) — the precise gap Canon fills; confirmed YouTube Data API v3 is free at 10,000 units/day (relevant only for metadata top-ups, not required at runtime); confirmed the HN Algolia API is free, keyless and 10k req/hr, which makes the weekly refresh real; found the HackerTube HN thread at 1,716 points / 452 comments, the strongest available evidence of audience appetite and the obvious launch venue; checked awesome-talks-style prior art (static GitHub lists, never ranked or tracked) and Tech Talks Weekly (new talks, not a canon); and found in-browser Google Takeout watch-history parsers already working client-side, which is what made the auto-tick feature safe to promise. Noted a licence caution: HN comment text is not clearly licensed for redistribution, so the build quotes one line and links back.
Sharpening pot (4/4): spent inside the deep-research answers above on the two changes — the weekly-refresh mechanism (Algolia, free) and the Takeout auto-tick (client-side, precedent exists) — plus the two prior-art checks that confirmed neither feature already exists for this audience.
Sharpening (7.2 to 8): Round 1 — weakest criterion: usefulness (5, a one-time toy: "browse the HN canon" is read-once). Change: made the canon finite and ranked (top 250 by distinct recommenders) and added a personal completion layer — localStorage ticks, a completion dial, and a weekly Monday arrival driven by a nightly HN Algolia re-query. Research: confirmed HackerTube has no recommendation-count ranking, no watched marker and no weekly arrivals feed (only a "recently recommended" sort), and that the Algolia HN API is free with a 10k req/hr limit and no key, so the weekly refresh is real and costs nothing. Also confirmed Tech Talks Weekly covers NEW talks only, not a canon. Usefulness 5 → 7 (capped at 7: nobody has proven weekly return for this audience). Shareability 6 → 8, since the output became a personal number rather than a catalog.

Round 2 — weakest criterion: wow (6: a checklist you fill in by hand is work, not wow). Change: added the Google Takeout drop-zone — drop watch-history.json, parsed entirely in-browser, and the canon auto-ticks itself, so the user's score appears without typing anything. Research: confirmed Takeout exports YouTube watch history as watch-history.json/html with video URLs and that in-browser Takeout parsers already exist and work client-side (smallwebapps.com/apps/tubetrace, github.com/topics/google-takeout), so this is buildable with no backend and no API key. Also checked for an existing "I've seen X/100" card tool for tech lists and found none — iCheckMovies/Letterboxd prove the behaviour in film, nothing equivalent for talks. Wow 6 → 8, buildability held at 8 (dataset schema still unverified, so not 9).
prototype_summary: An interactive dark-library prototype of "Canon" where users tick off the 250 videos HN recommends most, watch a completion dial climb, simulate importing YouTube Takeout history to auto-mark 6 watched talks, and generate a shareable canon card.
